name: Indonesia
hierarchy: Undang-Undang (UU, law);Perppu (emergency regulation in lieu of law);Peraturan Pemerintah (PP, government regulation);Peraturan Presiden (Perpres, presidential regulation);Peraturan Menteri (Permen, ministerial regulation);Keputusan Menteri (Kepmen, ministerial decision)
intro: Indonesia's electricity supply is provided principally by the state utility PLN, under the licensing framework of the 2009 Electricity Law. Most operational rules are ministerial regulations of the Ministry of Energy and Mineral Resources (ESDM), while presidential regulations set broader policy, including renewable pricing and the retirement of coal-fired plants.

name: Vietnam
hierarchy: Luật (law, National Assembly);Nghị quyết (resolution, National Assembly);Nghị định (decree, Government);Quyết định (decision, Prime Minister);Thông tư (circular, ministry)
intro: Vietnam's electricity sector is led by the state utility EVN. The 2024 Electricity Law replaced the 2004 law from 1 February 2025 and was followed by implementing decrees in 2025 on direct PPAs, renewable energy and rooftop solar. Investment in generation follows power development plans (PDP) approved by the Prime Minister.

name: Thailand
hierarchy: Act (Phra Ratchabanyat, law);Emergency Decree (Phra Ratchakamnot, law);Royal Decree (Phra Ratchakrit-sadika, decree);Ministerial Regulation (Kot Krasuang, ministerial regulation);Ministry notification (ประกาศกระทรวง, ministerial regulation);ERC regulation and notification (ระเบียบ/ประกาศ กกพ., regulator determination);Cabinet, NEPC and EPAC resolution (มติ, decision)
sources: EPPO resolutions database (NEPC and EPAC)|https://reso.eppo.go.th/main;Royal Thai Government Gazette|https://ratchakitcha.soc.go.th/;Energy Regulatory Commission (ERC)|https://www.erc.or.th/;Energy Policy and Planning Office (EPPO)|https://www.eppo.go.th/
intro: Thailand's electricity sector follows an enhanced single-buyer model: the state utility EGAT operates the transmission grid and purchases electricity from independent and small power producers, which it resells to the distribution utilities MEA (Bangkok) and PEA (the rest of the country). Policy is set mainly through resolutions of the National Energy Policy Council (NEPC) and its Energy Policy Administration Committee (EPAC), which the Energy Regulatory Commission (ERC) implements through regulations and notifications under the 2007 Energy Industry Act. Generation investment follows power development plans (PDP) approved by the NEPC.

name: Philippines
hierarchy: Republic Act (RA, law);Executive Order (EO, presidential regulation);DOE Department Circular (DC, circular);ERC Resolution (Res., decision);DOE Advisory (advisory)
sources: Department of Energy issuances|https://doe.gov.ph/laws-and-issuances/issuances;UP Law Center National Administrative Register (NARO)|https://naro.law.upd.edu.ph/;Energy Regulatory Commission (ERC)|https://www.erc.gov.ph/;Supreme Court E-Library|https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/
intro: The Philippine electricity sector was restructured under the 2001 Electric Power Industry Reform Act (EPIRA): generation and supply are competitive, while transmission (operated by NGCP) and distribution (private utilities and electric cooperatives) remain regulated, and the WESM spot market covers the three main grids. Policy instruments typically come in pairs: a Department of Energy (DOE) circular that sets policy and an Energy Regulatory Commission (ERC) resolution that gives it binding effect and sets prices. The 2008 Renewable Energy Act provides the basis for renewable portfolio standards, green energy auctions, the Green Energy Option and net metering.

name: Malaysia
hierarchy: Akta (Act of Parliament, law);Enakmen/Ordinan (Sabah enactment or Sarawak ordinance, law);Peraturan/Perintah, P.U.(A) (subsidiary legislation, government regulation);Pemberitahuan, P.U.(B) (Gazette notification, decision);Kod ST (Energy Commission code, code);Garis Panduan ST (Energy Commission guideline, regulator determination)
sources: Energy Commission legislation library|https://www.st.gov.my/ms/tentang-kami/perundangan;Laws of Malaysia (AGC)|https://lom.agc.gov.my/;SEDA|https://www.seda.gov.my/;Energy Commission of Sabah|https://ecos.gov.my/
intro: In Peninsular Malaysia, electricity is supplied by the vertically integrated utility TNB, which contains a ring-fenced Single Buyer and Grid System Operator, under the Electricity Supply Act 1990; Sabah and Sarawak have separate systems governed by state law. Most operational rules are binding Energy Commission guidelines, which are revised in place, often several times a year, while charges, quotas and procurement rounds are frequently first announced by the energy ministry (PETRA). The National Energy Transition Roadmap (2023) sets long-term targets, including 70% renewable installed capacity by 2050 and no new coal-fired plants.

name: India
hierarchy: Act of Parliament (law);Rules and statutory orders (S.O./G.S.R.) of the Central Government (government regulation);Regulations of CERC and other regulators (regulator determination);Ministry orders, office memoranda and guidelines (ministerial regulation);Cabinet-approved schemes and missions (decision);Press Notes of DPIIT (circular);National plans of CEA (plan)
sources: Gazette of India (eGazette)|https://egazette.gov.in/;India Code|https://www.indiacode.nic.in/;Press Information Bureau|https://www.pib.gov.in/;Ministry of New and Renewable Energy|https://mnre.gov.in/;Ministry of Power|https://powermin.gov.in/;Central Electricity Regulatory Commission|https://cercind.gov.in/;Central Board of Indirect Taxes and Customs|https://www.cbic.gov.in/;Directorate General of Trade Remedies|https://www.dgtr.gov.in/;Ministry of Heavy Industries|https://heavyindustries.gov.in/;Ministry of Mines|https://mines.gov.in/;DPIIT|https://dpiit.gov.in/
intro: Electricity is a concurrent subject under the Constitution: the Electricity Act, 2003 is administered by the Ministry of Power and the Central Electricity Authority, with the Central and State Electricity Regulatory Commissions setting tariffs and access rules, while renewable energy policy sits with the Ministry of New and Renewable Energy. Clean-technology industrial policy is spread across ministries: MNRE for solar manufacturing and the ALMM, Heavy Industries for EV and battery schemes, Mines for critical minerals, Finance for customs and trade-remedy duties on DGTR recommendations, and DPIIT for foreign investment policy. Most binding instruments are published in the Gazette of India as S.O. or G.S.R. notifications in Hindi and English.
